_comment: SURGX shared hepatopancreatobiliary steps: upper abdominal access, intra-operative ultrasound and cholangiography, hepatoduodenal ligament dissection, the Pringle manoeuvre, bile leak testing and the major haemorrhage bail-out. Used by two or more of open and subtotal cholecystectomy, laparoscopic bile duct exploration, splenectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy and right hepatectomy. Procedure-only steps stay in each procedure's steps_local.

step.hpb.upper-access.title: Upper abdominal incision and fixed retraction
step.hpb.upper-access.why: Upper abdominal organs sit high under the costal margin. Exposure here comes from the incision and a fixed retractor, not from an assistant pulling harder. Poor exposure is the root of most bleeding and duct injuries in open hepatobiliary surgery.
how: Choose the incision for the operation: right subcostal (Kocher) for the gallbladder and bile duct; bilateral subcostal (rooftop or chevron), a reversed L (J) or an upper midline for the liver and pancreas.
Divide the rectus and the oblique muscles with diathermy, ligating the superior epigastric vessels; preserve the intercostal nerves at the lateral end where possible.
Divide the ligamentum teres between ties and the falciform ligament up towards the suprahepatic veins, staying on the anterior abdominal wall.
Place a fixed costal-margin retractor (for example a ring or bar retractor) that lifts the costal margins upwards and cephalad, then pack the hepatic flexure and duodenum down.
When converting from laparoscopy, extend or join port sites rather than making a separate small incision that will not give the view you need.
structuresAtRisk: Superior epigastric vessels
Intercostal nerves (denervation of the rectus)
Liver capsule under the retractor blades
pitfalls: A short subcostal incision that forces deep retraction on the liver and tears its capsule.
Retractor blades placed on the liver itself rather than on the costal margin, causing capsular tears that ooze for the rest of the case.
Dividing the falciform ligament close to the liver where it bleeds from small parenchymal vessels.

step.hpb.ious.title: Intra-operative ultrasound before committing
step.hpb.ious.why: Pre-operative imaging is a map made weeks ago. Intra-operative ultrasound finds small metastases, shows the relationship of a tumour to the hepatic veins, portal pedicles and mesenteric vessels, and can change the operation before anything irreversible has been done.
how: Scan the whole liver systematically, segment by segment, before any mobilisation that alters its shape.
Trace the hepatic veins to the vena cava and the portal pedicles to the hilum, and mark the relevant vessels on the liver surface with diathermy.
For a pancreatic head tumour, assess its relationship to the superior mesenteric vein, portal vein and superior mesenteric artery, and look for liver metastases not seen on CT.
State what the scan has changed, if anything, to the team before proceeding.
structuresAtRisk: Middle hepatic vein
Portal vein and superior mesenteric vein
Left portal pedicle (the future remnant's inflow)
pitfalls: Scanning only the known lesion and missing a small contralateral metastasis that makes the resection futile.
Scanning after mobilisation, when the liver has rotated and the landmarks are distorted.
Treating ultrasound as optional when the pre-operative imaging is old or after chemotherapy.

step.hpb.cholangiogram.title: Intra-operative cholangiography
step.hpb.cholangiogram.why: A cholangiogram shows the anatomy of the ducts and any stones within them. It cannot prevent an injury on its own, but it can reveal a misidentified duct before it is divided and it answers whether the common bile duct needs clearing.
how: Flush the catheter and tubing to remove every air bubble; bubbles mimic stones.
Cannulate the cystic duct through a small ductotomy (or, when the triangle is obliterated, inject through the gallbladder), and secure the catheter with a clip or a loop.

Inject dilute contrast under fluoroscopy and look for: filling of the common hepatic duct and both left and right hepatic ducts, free flow into the duodenum, filling defects, and the length and insertion of the cystic duct.
If the right or left hepatic ducts do not fill, or the image does not make anatomical sense, stop and reconsider what has been cannulated.
Save the images and record the findings in the note.
structuresAtRisk: Common bile duct (if it is the duct cannulated)
Cystic duct (tearing at the ductotomy)
pitfalls: Accepting a cholangiogram that fills only the distal duct: that pattern can mean the catheter is in the common bile duct, not the cystic duct.
Air bubbles read as stones, prompting an unnecessary duct exploration.
Too concentrated contrast, which hides small stones.

step.hpb.hepatoduodenal.title: Dissecting the hepatoduodenal ligament
step.hpb.hepatoduodenal.why: The hepatoduodenal ligament carries the inflow of the whole liver: the bile duct, the hepatic artery and the portal vein. Arterial anatomy varies often, and a replaced or accessory hepatic artery divided by mistake can devascularise the liver or the bile duct anastomosis.
how: Palpate the ligament between finger and thumb before dissecting, feeling for a pulse behind the bile duct on the right, which suggests a replaced right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery.
Open the peritoneum over the ligament and identify the common bile duct anterolaterally, the hepatic artery medially and the portal vein posteriorly.
Sling each structure only after it has been positively identified and followed to where it goes; label what you sling aloud.
Before dividing any artery, test-clamp it and confirm a pulse persists in the artery that will supply the remnant.
structuresAtRisk: Replaced or accessory right hepatic artery
Proper and left hepatic arteries
Portal vein
Bile duct blood supply at 3 and 9 o'clock
pitfalls: Assuming textbook anatomy because the CT report did not mention a variant.
Skeletonising the bile duct circumferentially well above the planned division line, which devascularises it and leads to anastomotic stricture.
Dividing an artery before the test clamp, with no way back if the liver loses its pulse.

step.hpb.pringle.title: Pringle manoeuvre: sling, clamp, time, release
step.hpb.pringle.why: Occluding the hepatoduodenal ligament stops hepatic arterial and portal inflow. It reduces bleeding during liver transection and turns uncontrolled haemorrhage from the liver bed or a hepatic artery branch into a field where the bleeding point can be seen and repaired. It does not stop hepatic venous back-bleeding.
how: Open the lesser omentum, pass a finger through the foramen of Winslow (epiploic foramen) behind the ligament, and place a sling or tape around it before you need it.
Clamp by tightening the tourniquet or with a soft vascular clamp, tell the anaesthetist and start a clock; call out the time at intervals.
Use intermittent clamping for elective transection, with periods of release between clamping intervals per the unit protocol, and release fully when the transection is complete.
In an emergency, compression of the ligament between finger and thumb gives the same control while a sling is placed.

If bleeding continues despite a good Pringle, the source is hepatic venous or caval, or there is an aberrant left hepatic artery in the lesser omentum: lower the central venous pressure and look for these.
structuresAtRisk: Portal vein and hepatic artery (clamp injury)
Aberrant left hepatic artery in the lesser omentum
Liver function in the cirrhotic or chemotherapy-injured liver
pitfalls: Forgetting the clamp is on, or not recording the total ischaemic time.
Assuming a Pringle will control back-bleeding from the hepatic veins.
Long continuous clamping of a cirrhotic liver without discussion with the anaesthetist and the operating consultant.

step.hpb.bile-leak-check.title: Checking for bile leakage before closure
step.hpb.bile-leak-check.why: Bile leaks are among the commonest complications of biliary and liver surgery. A leaking duct seen on the table costs a stitch; the same leak found as a biloma on day five costs a drain, an ERCP and sometimes a re-operation.
how: Dry the operative field and place a clean white swab against the raw surface, duct closure or anastomosis for a minute, then inspect it for yellow or green staining.
After liver resection, consider a formal leak test where available, injecting saline, air or a fat emulsion through the cystic duct stump and watching the cut surface.
Suture visible leaking ducts with a fine monofilament rather than diathermising them.
Check the bile duct closure or hepaticojejunostomy along its whole circumference, including the back wall where it can be seen.
structuresAtRisk: Remnant bile ducts on the cut surface
Bile duct closure or anastomosis
pitfalls: Treating a negative swab test as proof that no leak will occur: necrosis of a cauterised duct leaks days later.
Diathermising a leaking duct, which seals it briefly and then sloughs.

step.hpb.major-bleed.title: Major haemorrhage: press, tell, call, then repair or pack
step.hpb.major-bleed.why: In upper abdominal surgery the large veins (portal, superior mesenteric, splenic, hepatic and the cava) tear rather than cut, and clamping blindly makes a small hole large. Survival depends on immediate pressure, early communication and the decision to stop and pack when physiology fails, not on finding the bleeding point quickly.
how: Put pressure on the bleeding: a finger, a swab on a stick or packs, and hold it. Do not clamp or clip into a pool of blood.
Tell the anaesthetist clearly, ask for the major haemorrhage protocol to be activated if blood loss is heavy, and ask for a second experienced surgeon, a cell saver and vascular instruments.
Improve exposure while holding pressure: suction, extend the incision, a second sucker, mobilise to get proximal and distal control.

Liver bleeding: Pringle for inflow, lower the central venous pressure for back-bleeding, and compress the liver between hands. Splenic bleeding: compress the hilum and complete the splenectomy. Mesenteric venous bleeding: digital control, then repair with fine monofilament.
If the patient becomes cold, acidotic or coagulopathic, stop: pack, close temporarily and plan a return after resuscitation (damage control).
structuresAtRisk: Portal vein and superior mesenteric vein
Splenic vein
Hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava
Adjacent bile duct and pancreas from blind suturing
pitfalls: Blind clamping or deep suturing into a field of blood, which converts a bleed into a bile duct or pancreatic injury.
Continuing to operate on a physiologically exhausted patient to finish the planned operation.
Not telling the anaesthetist until the blood pressure has already fallen.
